commits.subject: The Chronicle learns its own birthday
commits.lede: `npm run stamp && npm run chronicle`, now that the page has a commit to read. It is the fifty-third world and the newest line in its own history: born 2026-08-14, one commit, one hand.

commits.subject: The Chronicle: every world, in the order it appeared
commits.lede: The vibeverse has fifty-two worlds and no memory of building any of them. `/game` shows what exists and the passport shows where you have been; nothing has ever shown how the place came to be. This is that — and it writes itself, out of git, so it is exactly as true as the repository and cannot drift from it. Add a world and it writes itself a line here.

commits.subject: The form fills itself in while you type
commits.lede: Pasting a link was a leap of faith: you pressed Submit and only then found out what we had decided your game was called. Now the card fills in underneath the field, which is the same information a beat earlier and the difference between a form and a conversation.

commits.subject: Hats that are actually on the head, and three more of them
commits.lede: Hats were parented to the model holder at a fixed 1.78 m — "just above a ~1.85 m model's head" — which is true of a character standing still and of nothing else. Every character in the catalogue is a different GLB fitted to the same overall height, so their heads sit at different places inside it: the same number floats over a short one and cuts through a tall one. And because the mount never moved, the hat stayed bo

commits.subject: The city's controls fit on one row
commits.lede: Ten chips wanting 752px, and the strip holding them was never wider than half the screen — so three rows at 900px and two at 1440px.

commits.subject: Swimming, and snow that settles
commits.lede: Two things you could see the world wanting the moment it had a beach.

commits.subject: Vibe Island stops showing you somebody else's screen first
commits.lede: Clicking Vibe Island painted the character picker for a beat, then a loading screen, then the island. Same for Powder Peak, the moon, Mars, TJ's, Vibestar and the mines — half the world list is a `/city?spawn=…` link, so this was most of what "going to a world" looked like.

commits.subject: The avatar is the character's actual face
commits.lede: The chip in the corner has always shown an emoji — 🤖 for Vibey, 🦀 for Pinch — which identifies a species rather than a character. Sixty-three characters are built from one rig and photographed from it, so the corner can show the one you picked.

commits.subject: Submit a game without leaving the shelf
commits.lede: "Add yours →" and "Put your game here" both sent you to `/build`, which is a page about the deal rather than the form — so acting on the invitation meant two navigations away from the thing that made you want to. The arcade shelf is the argument for submitting; a form on its own route has to make that argument again from scratch.

commits.subject: Powered by creators, owned by players
commits.lede: The old arcade's line, back above the wordmark. "Every builder grows the universe" said one half of it — anybody can add a door — and stopped there. This one says the other half too: what you earn behind the door is yours. It is the claim /manifesto spends a page on ("Build worlds. Share ownership. Play forever.") in six words, in the slot a tagline goes.

commits.subject: The picker gets an exit, and one card width
commits.lede: Three things wrong with the search overlay, all of them mine from two commits ago when I gave it a way to open without looking at what opening it revealed.

Every object was fine. The town was not a town.

commits.subject: The paper moves into the hole beside the headline
commits.lede: At 1440×800 the first card row started at 558px and was cut off by the bottom of the window — you could not see one whole card without scrolling, on the page whose entire job is showing you the room. This file's own comment has said so for a while: every line of hero copy above the fold is a game the visitor did not see.

It has been finished for a long time and nothing in the app could open it: `GlobalNav` holds the state and the only thing it ever does with it is set it to `false`. The menu that used to open it was removed and the component was left behind — a whole f

commits.subject: The front door gets a sky, a cast, and a way in

commits.subject: The wink arrives as a picture, then wakes up
commits.lede: The mark on /coin has been a live three.js object for a while and the mark everywhere else has been a PNG, and each was right about something. The render is the real artwork and it paints in one frame off the image cache; the object turns, catches the light differently every second, and can react to things — and costs three.js, a GLB and a WebGL context to say so.

commits.subject: The boss's shard was a white plate, not a gem
commits.lede: At 2.4× scale an additive white icosahedron at 0.95 opacity blows out into a flat slab the size of the boss's head. Smaller, amber, dimmer, and turning — a piece of God Orb it is carrying rather than a hole in the render.

commits.subject: mines-probe: survive an HMR reload instead of dying on it
commits.lede: Editing a source file while the probe is up sends vite's hot reload through page.evaluate, which throws "execution context was destroyed" and killed the run seconds before its summary. One skipped sample is the right response.

commits.subject: 254 MB of models becomes 70 MB, and nothing looks different
commits.lede: None of the .glb files in this repo had ever been through an optimiser. floating-island.glb was 38.7 MB and 1,049,034 triangles — for a decorative island that renders about 300 px wide behind a menu. That is a frame-rate problem on every phone that opens the hub before it is a download problem, and it is simply what a Meshy export looks like when nobody runs the last step.

So these are three new body plans first and fourteen designs second.

commits.lede: The portal could always frame somebody else's game; what it could not do was let them ask. Getting in meant knowing Jack and waiting for a migration, and the schema said as much in a comment: "flip this when the submit form lands."

commits.lede: Character prices live in this repo twice on purpose: once in `characterShop.ts` so the shelf can print an honest number before you pay, and once in the `vibe-economy` edge function, which is the copy that actually charges. Adding stock therefore needs a function deploy as well as a push — and pushing does not deploy functions here, which I had assumed and checked and had wrong in that order.

commits.lede: The presses have not missed a day — issues 3, 4 and 5 came out at 05:32, 13:00 and 06:25 — but the schedule was one shot at 13:00 UTC, and one shot is a design that loses a whole day to a bad minute. A timeout, an OpenRouter blip, a cold start that runs long: nothing retries, and the front door goes on quietly showing yesterday.

commits.lede: Everything on the shelf was one biped. You could change the palette, the ears, the cape and the wings and still get twelve characters who are indistinguishable in a doorway at thirty metres, because a silhouette is mostly *how a thing moves* and every one of them moved identically — same hips, same two legs, same stride solver.

commits.subject: The teammate can shoot back
commits.lede: It has spent every match so far as a very loyal 4 m of scenery: it followed, it called out, it talked, and it could not take a single point of dryness off anyone. Now that ghosts are real damage targets and `hit` carries damage, it has the same soaker everyone else does.

commits.subject: Players can finally soak each other
commits.lede: SPLASH ROYALE shipped without player-versus-player water. Not throttled, not buggy — absent. No client ever sent a shot, `shot` and `splash` existed in the protocol and were never emitted by a weapon, ghosts were never registered as damage targets, and the two systems that did consume `splash` used it for a decal and some particles. Two people in a lobby could see each other, chat, glue each other's ankles and announ

commits.subject: The teammate went deaf after the first finished match
commits.lede: Watched live tonight, three times: jack joins, the log says "jack is on the field (dolphin)", and the next status line reads `peers 1, following —`. The bot could see him and would not follow him.

commits.subject: The end card says Play again
commits.lede: "Get wet again" is a joke that only lands once, and the button it is on is the one you press when you want another match — not the one you press to be told what the mode is called. Jack asked for the plain word.

commits.subject: The teammate could not reach a squad that was still on the bus
commits.lede: Tonight's match, from the bot's log: spawned beside Jack, then "stuck — taking a detour" every three seconds for six minutes, pinned at x -1230, 866 m away, until the match ended. Jack never saw it. Two bugs stacked.

commits.subject: Escape gives the mouse back instead of throwing you out
commits.lede: Escape is the only way a browser hands the cursor back, and the lobby veil was keyed on pointer lock alone. That conflated "has not joined yet" with "has joined and wants their mouse", so every player who pressed it got the full entry screen — room code, roster, drop-in button — slammed over a match that was still running underneath. It read as being kicked to the lobby. Nothing had stopped.

It does not cover the case that actually happens, which is worse for being quieter: a clone deep enough to have *some* history presents its graft boundary as the commit that created every file in the tree. So `git log -- src/pages/About.tsx` answers, confide

The arm now hangs off the BUS, look input orbits it, and a keep-out ellipsoid containing the whole rig — hull, balloon and riders — is solved along the look axis so it can never end up inside again. Somebody reading it now and wanting to add a friend's game would follow it and vendor the game, which is the trade we took exactly once and should not take again by default.

commits.lede: Every world in here is a file in this repository, which caps how many there can ever be at how much of Jack's week is free. That does not scale to "my friend made a game", and it does not scale to an eight-year-old with an idea.
